17208-the-tales-of-mother-goose-as-first:
Charles Perrault first gathered these tales in 1696, and Charles Welsh made this new translation, with an introduction by M. V. O'Shea and pictures after Gustave Dore. Cinderella and her glass slipper leads, followed by Sleeping Beauty, Little Thumb, Puss in Boots, Riquet of the Tuft, Blue Beard, The Fairy, and Little Red Riding-Hood.

The tales keep their old morals and their sharp edges: wolves, ogres, and cruel husbands sit beside kind fairies and clever cats. Welsh's plain English and Dore-based pictures suit family reading. This is a fine first Perrault for children and adults who want the classic tales close to their first French form.
24745-the-loss-of-the-kent-east-indiaman:
General Sir Duncan MacGregor wrote this account as a letter to a friend, telling how the East Indiaman Kent burned in the Bay of Biscay. The ship left the Downs bound for Bengal and China with 641 people aboard: soldiers of the 31st Regiment, their wives and children, passengers, and crew. Fire broke out at sea, and the days that followed tested every soul on board.

MacGregor, then in his nineties when he revised the tale, stresses calm courage, order amid panic, and the rescue that saved so many. The letter reads as both a sea story and a sermon on providence under fire. It remains a vivid firsthand account of one of the great ship disasters of the sailing age.
35459-the-strange-story-of-harper-s-ferr:
Joseph Barry told the strange tale of Harper's Ferry and its lore. Barry dwelt in the place for half a span of years times ten. The first print came out in 1903 at Martinsburg. Club women of the town kept the book in print for years. Six prints of it ran through the last age's mid years.

John Brown's raid made the town's name known to all lands. Barry sets that tale down from long home at the spot. Ghost lore and old tales of the hills round it share the book. Rivers, arms works, and war years fill its past in turn. Town past fans get a dweller's own store of fact. Each tale is short and full of place.
38235-the-gentleman-s-model-letter-write:
Gentleman's Model Letter Writer is a complete guide to correspondence on all subjects. Frederick Warne and Company published it in London and New York. A preface grants that letter writers are many, yet a want remains. Compilers drew with great care from several sources for this manual. Much original matter fills gaps that experience showed to be real.

Contents model a book keeper applying for employment as a first case. Letters acknowledge congratulation on the birth of a child in due form. A father asks a school principal for terms for his son's place. A gentleman seeks a loan on the insurance of his life in print. Offers for property, replies, and corn trade letters fill the manual out.
42809-a-treatise-on-the-incubus-or-night:
John Waller wrote a treatise on the incubus, or night-mare, printed at London in 1816. Waller was a surgeon of the Royal Navy, the title page says. His full title adds disturbed sleep, terrific dreams, and nocturnal visions. It promises the means of removing these distressing complaints. The introduction ranks sound sleep among heaven's greatest blessings to mankind.

Undisturbed sleep is one of the best signs of perfect health, he holds. Any disturbance of it proves some derangement in the animal economy. A slight falling off from health may be read in sleep and dreams. Before an epidemic fever, patients complain of frightful dreams, he notes. No other sign of sickness may yet be perceived, he adds. Frightful dreams are often forerunners of dangerous and fatal diseases. Waller gives a surgeon's counsel on the terrors of the night.
44609-the-northfield-tragedy-or-the-robb:
The Northfield Tragedy is a pamphlet history by Hanson, published at St Paul, Minnesota, in 1876, the year of the crime it records. Its long title promises the whole story: the bank attempt, the murders, and the great manhunt.

Hanson begins by laying out the work, as he calls it. Between late August and early September 1876 a company of strangers drifted through Minnesota towns. They passed as Texas cattle dealers, land speculators and railroad surveyors, registering at the best hotels under names like King, Ward and Huddleston, and spending freely. Their audacity and southern speech marked them as no ordinary persons. The pamphlet, rushed out while the James and Younger gang's raid was fresh, is instant history with biographies of victims, captors and desperadoes attached.
55073-the-trial-of-aaron-burr:
Joseph Brady, clerk of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, wrote an account of the trial of Aaron Burr, issued in New York in 1913. Chief Justice Marshall fronts the book, and plates show the warrant for Burr's arrest and the subpoena served on President Jefferson.

Burr arrived in Richmond on the evening of March 26, 1807, under a guard of nine men, and was lodged in the Eagle Tavern. On March 30 he was handed to the civil authorities on Marshall's warrant. The first hearing was private, with Attorney General Rodney and counsel Wickham and Randolph present. Depositions from Generals Eaton and Wilkinson tied Burr to the charge.
57594-the-western-echo-a-description-of-:
The Western Echo is a wagon tour of the West by George Romspert. The United Brethren house at Dayton issued it in 1881. Its full title promises a survey of states and territories. Sketches list a prairie fire and a mountain lake. The tour starts from Dayton, Ohio. Coal mines, Indianapolis, and Illinois roads come first. The party crosses into Iowa and Missouri. Kansas City and the Des Moines valley follow.

Omaha opens the plains chapters. Homestead land and cold winds mark the Platte valley. Buffalo herds, a wolf hunt, and a blizzard crowd chapter three. A frozen man is found on the trail. The southern trip crosses Indian agencies and the Red River. Santa Fe and the Sierra Nevada close the range. Romspert writes as a plain witness of the new West.
57686-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Robert Barr is a finding aid to one author shelf. It lists Barr novels and story sets held by Project Gutenberg in plain order. A Rock in the Baltic leads, with The Face and the Mask and The Strong Arm next. Jennie Baxter Journalist, The Sword Maker, and the Eugene Valmont triumphs stand in the list.

Tables of contents for each volume follow the master list in the file. Chapter heads for A Rock in the Baltic open at an incident at the bank. Readers can scan Barr whole range, from steamer chair tales to Stranleigh novels, at a glance. The index serves as a map to a once popular storyteller works.
58440-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Amelia Barr is a catalogue compiled by David Widger. It lists the novels of Amelia Edith Huddleston Barr held in that digital library, title by title. Remember the Alamo heads the contents, followed by The Man Between and The Maid of Maiden Lane. Historical romance in Texas, Scotland, and old New York fills her shelf.

Later heads include her autobiography, All the Days of My Life, among the tales. Barr wrote scores of popular novels in a long career, and this index serves as a map to the free editions of them. Readers who find one Barr novel here can find the rest at a glance. It is a finding list, not a narrative.
6028-opening-a-chestnut-burr:
E. P. Roe sends out his fourth venture, a simple October story, with few words of preface. He has taken well-deserved criticism from gentlemen of the caustic pen without hard feeling, and wonders they found so much to praise. How critics judge this newcomer he leaves to the future.

Roe pictures his true readers around glowing hearths in quiet homes like those he describes. He hopes the book will be welcomed for the sake of its predecessors and may make friends of its own. Letters from every class and corner of the country encouraged him. The novel offers homely warmth for autumn evenings.
63826-spider-men-of-gharr:
Spider Men of Gharr is a science fiction tale by Wilbur Peacock, taken from Planet Stories for summer 1945. Its blurb names Kimball Trent the last hope of a ravaged Earth. Secrets locked in his mind would free the Barbs. He lacks only the key to the blue monsters who cannot die.

The tale opens in cold and darkness. Kim wakes in a cave, unable to move or open his eyes, his thoughts slow as molasses. Heat bites into his numbed flesh like a naked yellow flame. He clings to his own name as his only reality. The cave is artificial, with shelves of dull gleaming objects and man-hewn blocks of stone. Peacock builds a lost world underground.
britannica-1911-barr:
Barr is a town of Germany, in the imperial province of Alsace-Lorraine, on the Kirneck stream, thirteen miles north of Schlettstadt by rail. Its position in a wine country shapes the whole short notice that the 1911 Britannica entry gives it.

The town has an Evangelical church and a Roman Catholic church. Considerable tanneries work there, turning hides with the bark the district affords. An active trade runs in two goods, wine and timber, the valley's twin products. Its population in 1900 was 5,243. Nothing more is claimed: readers get a compact gazetteer entry covering place, churches, tanning, trade, and people, and no history at all.
britannica-1911-birr:
Birr, also called Parsonstown, is a market town of King's County, Ireland. It stands on a slope above the Birr river, 87 miles west-south-west of Dublin by rail. Its 1901 urban population was 4,438. Streets spread in regular form from Cumberland Square. A Doric column there holds a statue of the Duke of Cumberland, marking Culloden. Birr Castle, beside the town, is the place's great claim to fame in science.

William, third Earl of Rosse, built his great reflecting telescope at the castle between 1828 and 1845. The tube runs 56 feet long and weighs three tons, the 1911 Britannica entry says. A bronze statue of Lord Rosse stands in the town. St Brendan founded an abbey at Birr, and its parish church still bears his name. The castle was besieged under Cromwell and taken by Ireton in 1650. Corn, timber, brewing, and distilling fill out the town's trades.
britannica-1911-de-la-warr:
De la Warr is an English barony held by two linked families. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its tangled descent. A Roger de la Warr was called to Parliament in 1299. His line of men died out with the fifth baron in 1426.

The fifth baron half sister carried the claim to the West house. Her son took the La Warr title as a second founder. Later barons served Henry the Seventh and Henry the Eighth. One of them hosted the king at his rebuilt Sussex house. That lord spoke out against the pulling down of abbeys. Arrest followed, though pardon and release came soon after. His nephew tried to poison him to hasten inheritance. Parliament barred that nephew from the honors for the crime. Restoration came in 1563, and a new patent in 1570.
britannica-1911-ewing-juliana-horatia-or:
Juliana Horatia Orr Ewing lived from 1841 to 1885 and wrote for children. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Ecclesfield in Yorkshire, her birth place. She was the daughter of the Reverend Alfred Gatty and Margaret Gatty. One of a large brood, she told tales to her young kin. Her brother Alfred set music to the plays she staged at home.

She was well schooled in classics and in modern tongues alike. Verse by her ran in Aunt Judy's Magazine, her mother's journal from 1866. Tales such as The Land of Lost Toys first showed in that journal. In 1867 she wed Major Alexander Ewing, himself an author of note. Till her death in 1885 she wrote tale after tale for the young.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eliza-allen-s:
Eliza Allen Starr was an American writer and lecturer on art, born at Deerfield, Massachusetts, in 1824 and dead at Durand, Illinois, in 1901. Schooled at home, she traced her father's line to Dr. Comfort Starr, who settled at Cambridge in 1633. At thirteen she went to Boston, finished her studies in 1845, and opened a studio there, then moved to Brooklyn and Philadelphia and taught drawing at Natchez.

Meeting Bishop Kenrick in Philadelphia stirred a faith already in her heart, and after nine years of struggle she was received into the Catholic Church at Boston on 23 December 1854. At Chicago from 1856 she found her life's work, writing books and illustrating them with her own pencil, lecturing across the United States, and giving ten lectures a year at home. Her books include Songs of a Lifetime, Patron Saints, Pilgrims and Shrines, and a life of Isabella of Castile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-curr:
Joseph Curr was an English priest remembered as a controversialist and a martyr of charity. Born at Sheffield late in the eighteenth century, he studied at Crook Hall and Ushaw College and served missions in Manchester, where he debated the Protestant Bible Association. After a retreat at La Trappe in France, he worked at Callaly, Blackburn, and Whitby.

In 1847, when typhus struck Leeds and priests were scarce, Curr volunteered for the stricken city and died of the fever on 29 June. His writings include a Sunday-school aid, translations from Liguori and Bourdaloue, and Familiar Instructions in Catholic Faith and Morality. Sermons and controversial pamphlets also survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-finbarr:
Finbarr, bishop and patron of Cork, evangelized Munster's towns before settling where Cork city now stands. Born near Bandon about 550, son of Amergin, he preached at Gowran, Coolcashin, and Aghaboe, founded a school at Eirce, and dwelt for years as a hermit at Gougane Barra. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cloyne to 25 September 623.

He was buried in the cathedral he built on the site of Cork, and honoured also at Dornoch and Barra in Scotland. A modern replica of Cormac's chapel now stands at Gougane Barra in his honour. Five Irish saints share his name, and the entry keeps this Finbarr, Lochan or Barr, distinct. The portrait is brief: preacher, school founder, hermit, and city patron in one life.
doe-osti-17168021-post-irradiation-exami:
Shaileyee Bhattacharya, Annabelle Le Coq, Matthew deJong, and Oak Ridge colleagues examine yttrium hydride samples after irradiation in the MIT reactor, in report ORNL/SPR-2026/4941 dated September 2026. Yttrium hydride is a moderator material of interest for compact fission surface power reactors. The samples rode in the Fission Surface Power campaign.

Chapters cover capsule disassembly and the examination plan. Methods include visual checks and mass measures, then heat property tests by laser flash and dilatometry, which track how the material conducts heat and expands. Further sections treat structure and chemistry changes from the neutron exposure. Findings feed design data for hydride moderated space and remote power units.
doe-osti-17197385-post-irradiation-exami: Yttrium hydrides after MITR got their exam again, and this DOE report covers the post-irradiation findings. The pages record the specimen results. The materials team gets its data. The exam was post-irradiation. The results were specimen. The team got data.
doe-osti-3798026-searching-for-the-most-:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-230151-2026-TECH, dated August 2026, hunts field errors that most harm beam stability in a key magnet. Santiago Franco de la Matta and Yun Luo are the printed authors. The B2PF magnet sits in the interaction region, where the beam swells to its largest size. Small flaws in its field can excite resonances and shrink the safe beam area. With eighteen error types in play, the harmful mix is hard to guess.

The team ran nearly thirty thousand simulations on the Brookhaven Linux cluster, varying all eighteen errors. Each run scored stability two ways: the dynamic aperture and the tune diffusion rate. Straight-line fits missed links that a learning model caught, so both methods were used. The work ranks which errors drive the losses and sets tolerance ranges for each.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HarrisLarryLSee:
Tom Belden wrote a viewpoint piece for the Dallas Morning News on November 22, 1977. His subject was the people who gather at Dealey Plaza. On the eve of the fourteenth anniversary of the assassination, doubters were assembling at the grassy knoll, the slope at the center of so many theories.

Anniversaries turned the plaza into a meeting place for the unconvinced. Belden, writing in the city's own paper, watched his hometown's wound become a yearly convention. The piece preserves how Dallas itself regarded the pilgrims who kept returning to the scene.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VanderKerr_Van_: Chapter III of a book on the assassination looks at how Dallas television and radio covered the killing on Friday, November 22, 1963. Local stations were the first to carry the news, often with confused early reports. The chapter studies their broadcasts as both journalism and historical record. For media history, few days show live local coverage under pressure as clearly as that Friday in Dallas.
opening-a-chestnut-burr:
Edward Payson Roe called this novel, his fourth book, a simple October story, and sent it out hoping it would enter homes the way his earlier ones had. In his preface he pictures readers around a glowing hearth in quiet houses, and says the book was really written for them. Its hero, he hints in verse, is like a great ship caught halfway across the sea with its stores run out.

Roe promises that the book's purpose will become clear as it is read, and that its incidents and characters are mainly imagined. The subject he writes on, the preface says, cannot be separated from happiness in this world or the next. Victorian readers made Roe one of the most popular novelists of his day.
the-tales-of-mother-goose-as-first-colle: Charles Welsh translated Charles Perrault's Tales of Mother Goose for D. C. Heath, working from Perrault's first collection of 1696, with an introduction by M. V. O'Shea and pictures after Gustave Doré. Merely the front pages and contents are present in this record, so none of the fairy tales themselves can be read here. The contents name eight stories, among them Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots, Blue Beard, and Little Red Riding-Hood. The list alone shows the core of the Mother Goose collection that shaped later fairy-tale books.
